articles.title: Pokemon’s Creators Are Ready to Officially Ditch a 30-Year-Old Series Tradition
articles.subtitle: Pokemon Champion was made to preserve the series' traditional gameplay It seems that big changes may be in store for the Pokémon formula.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Pokemon Champion was made to preserve the series' traditional gameplay

It seems that big changes may be in store for the Pokémon formula. In a recent talk between Pokémon battle director Shigeki Morimoto and Pokémon Champions game director Kazumasa Iwao, the former said a key reason Game Freak released Champions was to preserve a place for the series' traditional turn-based battles, implying even the mainline games may eventually ditch this approach.

In a translated statement posted by Centro Leaks on X, Iwao said, “One big reason [for Champions ]: the battle rules we’ve used through the Pokémon series for so long may gradually start changing as the series moves forward. And there are people who’ve been playing since Red and Green, Gold and Silver — decades. So just saying ‘battles have changed now play the new one’ didn’t feel right.”

Over the last few years, Game Freak has gone with a different approach in the spin-off Legends games ( Arceus and Z-A ), altering combat so players control their ‘mons in real-time, selecting attacks which then go on cooldown. While the Legends games are a significant departure, the mainline Pokémon titles have still been using the series’ turn-based approach, the most recent being 2022’s Scarlet and Violet.

Pokémon Winds and Waves are the next mainline series installments, and while Game Freak hasn’t officially announced if they will be turn-based or real-time, a tranche of 2024 leaks suggests that they will still be turn-based. However, the formula will likely change significantly, incorporating elements from Arceus and Z-A.

Earlier this year, Centro Leaks claimed that instead of being locked into a singles or doubles fight, opposing teams can change mid-battle, with additional opponents entering the fray. One alleged leaked image from the game shows a trainer battling nine Charizards. The game will also apparently introduce over 300 new 'mons, which would be almost double the series' previous high.

Game Freak released Pokémon Champions this April to a somewhat mixed initial reception. It’s a PvP battle sim where players create teams and duke it out online.

While the Pokémon competitive scene was a bit hostile to the game at first because it only featured a small subset of Pokémon, many eventually came around, accepting that it works as a great introduction to the competitive scene because it doesn’t include everything. Instead, players have been forced to create all-new teams that differ from Scarlet and Violet ’s meta.

The game’s monetization is also relatively forgiving for a free-to-play title, making it fairly easy to earn the in-game currency needed to build and train teams.

Still, Iwao’s comments likely struck a nerve, because there are many fans who love turn-based battles but aren’t interested in sweating it out online against a Charizard Y player who keeps using Heat Wave. While the mainline series will remain turn-based for the short term, it seems that may not be true forever.

Long before APFS, Mac OS X introduced the concept of purgeable space in storage, that currently occupied by files that could, when necessary, be deleted and used as free space. The bulk of this used to be caches and other files that were a convenience not a necessity. When APFS introduced snapshots that are used in Time Machine and other backups, they too were added to purgeable space, and Time Machine automatically purges its own snapshots when they’re more than 24 hours old.

Since High Sierra and APFS snapshots, accounting for purgeable space has been inconsistent and often misleading. I first reported this over eight years ago in Sierra 10.12.6 and High Sierra 10.13.3, and most recently three years ago in Ventura 13.3.1. This article looks at how this is handled now in Tahoe 26.6.2.

Conventionally, accessible storage Capacity is allocated to one of three categories

Available and not currently in use to store data,

Used to store data that macOS wants to retain,

Purgeable, as it’s currently used to store data that macOS can purge when it needs more free storage.

Then for any given storage device Capacity = Available + (Used – Purgeable)

There is disappointingly little documentation on space management in macOS, and the closest Apple comes to defining purgeable space is in Disk Utility’s Help pages, where it’s stated to be “space that macOS can free up when needed by removing files from your computer (you can’t manually remove the files that are designated purgeable, but macOS removes them as space is required)”.

On the face of it, that includes cache files but not snapshots, as they can be manually removed in Disk Utility, as I’ve discussed in detail here. This is contradicted when using tmutil localsnapshot to make Time Machine snapshots, which reports that “local snapshots are considered purgeable and may be removed at any time by deleted(8)”, as deleted is the purgeable space and cache management service in macOS.

APFS snapshots can also be created by third-party apps that have the appropriate restricted entitlement. Apple doesn’t explain whether those too can be purged by macOS when additional free space is required.

To demonstrate the purgeability of snapshots, it’s best to perform tests on an external disk formatted in APFS, containing no other data. For this I used the same procedure as previously to assess this in Ventura.

In outline, what this does is create a Time Machine snapshot of a volume containing files so large they almost fill the container, leaving little free space. The files are then deleted, leaving just the snapshot, and its purgeability tested by trying to copy another large file into that volume. That should force the snapshot to be purged to accommodate the new file.

Although you can do this using a single partition including the whole of the disk, it’s simplest to repartition the disk with a relatively small APFS container, such as 100 GB, using Disk Utility.

Add a second volume to your test container, also in plain APFS format. In this case, I have named those two volumes TestVolume1 and TestVolume2. Then write large files to TestVolume1 to almost fill the container. This time I copied across several large IPSW files totalling just over 94 GB. Inspect these using Disk Utility.

The container has a Capacity of 100 GB, with 94.92 GB Used and 5.08 GB Free, which is correct.

TestVolume1 has a Capacity of 100 GB, 5.08 GB Available, 94.8 GB Used, and 549 KB Purgeable, which also appears correct.

TestVolume2 has a Capacity of 100 GB, 5.08 GB Available with 860 KB used, 549 KB purgeable, and Other Volumes have 94.92 GB Used. Everything appears in order.

articles.content:
MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac.

The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.

MacPaw is teaming up with Liquid AI to bring more on-device AI to the Mac

Liquid AI’s Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) will be adapted for Mac-based assistance and combined with MacPaw’s own on-device technologies: Mnemos for memory and Elix for inference.

Eney already shifted to a local model last year, keeping reasoning, contextual search, skill execution, and conversation history on the device whenever possible.

The new partnership is intended to push that approach further. The two companies are jointly developing the underlying stack rather than MacPaw simply adding another third-party model.

Once the technology has been tested and implemented in Eney, MacPaw says it plans to bring it to more of its products. It also wants to make the shared AI stack available to Mac developers through Setapp.

That could let participating apps expose more of their capabilities and context to Eney. This would allow the assistant to understand what is inside an app. It could also provide more useful answers or take relevant actions.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Spilled coffee on your MacBook? This sleeve dries it out before it’s too late
articles.subtitle: Macworld Active-moisture rescue insurance for your tech This might just save the day (and your MacBook) Learn More (function () { document.querySelector("#sticky-promo-block a").addEventListener("click", function(e) { const debug =...
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
Active-moisture rescue insurance for your tech

This might just save the day (and your MacBook)

Every sensible MacBook owner recognizes that while their prized laptop can put up with the odd bump and nudge against a hard edge, it makes sense to protect it while on the move. That might mean picking one of the best MacBook backpacks or other carrying kit, but it might just be choosing a tight padded sleeve for it to nestle in, saving it from unintended impacts and possible scratches.

Another big danger for a MacBook outside the office or home is water. MacBooks are not water-resistant as Apple doesn’t build any ingress protection (IP) ratings into its laptops as it does its iPhone (IP68). I recently dived into a swimming pool with my iPhone 16 Pro in my pocket. I didn’t panic too much but I knew there was a possibility that damage could have been done despite the water-protection ranking.

Your backpack might be water resistant, but damage can still be done if water still gets into your laptop or other devices. Now a clever multi-function solution might just save your very wet day. UAG’s Dryout Ultimate Sleeve might rescue your MacBook, iPad, keyboard or storage device before any invasive moisture has more time to cause damage.

UAG

How to use the UAG Dryout Sleeve to dry your laptop

The sleeve is a secondary drying aid designed to draw out residual moisture; it is not a substitute for immediately shutting down, unplugging and draining the MacBook first.

Shut down the MacBook immediately. Don’t keep using it to check whether it still works.

Disconnect it from power and unplug any accessories. Electricity combined with moisture increases the risk of a short circuit and permanent damage.

Turn the MacBook keyboard-side down to help liquid drain out. Avoid shaking it, which could spread moisture further inside.

Wipe away visible liquid from the keyboard, case and ports with a clean, absorbent cloth.

Now place the MacBook inside the UAG Dryout Sleeve and close it so the moisture-removal material can work.

Leave the MacBook switched off while it dries. UAG recommends leaving it in the Dryout Sleeve for around 3–9 hours, but after a significant spill you should be prepared to keep the MacBook powered off for at least 24 hours.

Ways in which moisture can get into and damage your laptop

Desk accidents—such as beverage or vase spills—or working too close to a water source, for instance in a kitchen or even by a swimming pool, can too easily cause a gadget emergency. Weather exposure, where you are caught in heavy rain or snow while carrying your gear in a vulnerable bag, is an obvious situation we’ve all been in.

Few of us, however, consider the dangers of condensation—bringing your cold laptop into a warm, humid room can cause moisture droplets to form inside. I hate to mention it, but excessive sweating can also cause moisture to invade your tech gear, so maybe towel off after a workout, and certainly following a swim, before leaning over your laptop.

Keys are not airtight so liquid can flow directly through the key switches into the chassis. Side ports, such as USB and HDMI, provide a straight path to internal boards. Even vents for cooling fans and hinges can let moisture seep inside if placed on a wet surface or exposed to heavy rain.

articles.title: Open and move windows between displays automatically
articles.subtitle: When I was visiting my pal Myke Hurley in London last year, I noticed that he had a second display to the right of his main one.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
When I was visiting my pal Myke Hurley in London last year, I noticed that he had a second display to the right of his main one. It was large and mounted vertically, and when he recorded a podcast, he kept all his recording information over there. I liked the idea of monitoring my recordings while they were going on, just for extra peace of mind, and a second display seemed like the right way to do it.

If only I had a second display! But I do, of course, because my main Mac is now a MacBook Pro. So I’ve taken to recording podcasts using the “Hurley Method,” with my Audio Hijack windows positioned on the laptop display, off to my left.

It’s nice, but if you know me, I quickly became frustrated by the number of clicks and drags I needed to perform every single time I record a podcast: Open up my laptop, open Audio Hijack, open the list of recording sessions, double-click on the one I’m using right now, then drag the window over to the laptop display.

So today I automated it.

None of my automations work if I haven’t opened the laptop, and while it sits next to my Mac in a nice stand from Twelve South, it’s closed most of the time. So my first step before moving windows to the laptop display is to make sure that the display is available! Fortunately, there’s a command-line command for that:

If you want, you can simplify the output by piping it through a grep command like system_profiler SPDisplaysDataType | grep -B1 "Resolution", but all I really want to do is search for the text string “Built-in”, which indicates that the laptop is open and its built-in display is running.

I automate most of my recording stuff using Keyboard Maestro macros triggered by an Elgato Stream Deck. So I built my automation into an existing macro in Keyboard Maestro, just adding a new if/then statement: If the calculation `SCREENCOUNT() > 1 returns true.

Then the macro runs the shell script, saves that to a local variable called LocalScreens, and it’s time for one more if/then statement, to ensure that this part of the macro only runs when more than one screen is attached and when the internal MacBook Pro display is active.

Unfortunately, the next step requires automating Audio Hijack, and while that app is very scriptable via JavaScript, and controllable via Shortcuts (or a plain text file?!), there’s no direct method of automating it from within Keyboard Maestro. So I created a basic Shortcut containing the JavaScript required to tell Audio Hijack to open a specific session by name, with the name passed to the Shortcut as input:

Then it’s a one-step item in Keyboard Maestro to run that shortcut with the name of my Audio Hijack session as the input:

(I wish this was cleaner and I didn’t need to run a shortcut. The alternative is to literally write out a text file containing the JavaScript and run it via a shell script. Is that cleaner? Doesn’t feel like it, but it’s more self-contained and doesn’t rely on the good graces of Shortcuts.)

Now that I know that my MacBook Pro display is open and my Audio Hijack session window is open, it’s a one-step command in Keyboard Maestro to make the move:

This one’s a little tricky. I have to use the Move and Resize Window command, but instead of standard numerical values, I need to use custom “smart” values that Keyboard Maestro supports.

In this case, horizontally it’s SCREENVISIBLE(Internal,MidX)-600 —essentially, 600 pixels to the left of the midpoint of the internal display—and vertically it’s SCREENVISIBLE(Internal,MidY)-250 —250 pixels up from the midpoint of the display. You can play around with the dimensions until the window ends up in the right spot, and of course, at the right size.

And that was it. Now, when I press my recording button on my Stream Deck, if my laptop display is open, the session window will automatically pop open on my laptop display. I sure do like it when things happen on my computer automatically.

articles.title: Wispr Flow takes on AI meeting assistants with Notetaker, its first product beyond dictation

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker now available for Mac

If you’re unfamiliar with Wispr Flow, it is one of the leading voice-to-text AI tools for a growing number of users who feel comfortable using voice to compose messages, emails, documents, and other text instead of typing.

Granted, voice-based interactions are not practical in every environment. Still, Wispr Flow ’s rapidly growing user base (which the company said in March was expanding by 40% month over month) suggests that AI-powered dictation tools may become mainstream faster than many expected, or give them credit for.

Until now, Wispr has offered a single product, which polishes up messy speech and turns it into “clear, polished writing in every app.”

Today, the company is expanding its lineup with Notetaker, a smart, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcriber, and summarizer. The new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new item in the app’s left-hand sidebar.

As Wispr CEO and co-founder Tanay Kothari notes (no pun intended):

“Nobody reads meeting transcripts. But everyone acts on them. The transcript feeds the summary, the summary feeds the follow-up email, the recap goes to whoever missed the call. You’ve learned to give the notes a quick once-over before trusting them, because sometimes a name is wrong or an action item is assigned to the wrong person.”

In other words, while the transcript itself may have limited value to some, accurately extracting the key details, decisions, and action items from it can be more useful to a broader set of users.

Notetaker also briefs users before meetings by gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line linked to its source. More broadly, it draws context from calendars and connected apps such as Slack.

During meetings, Notetaker provides a live transcript so the user can quickly check back on what was said. Once the meeting ends, it processes the full recording again with additional context, which Wispr says improves the final transcript and the summaries, decisions, key dates, and action items generated from it.

Afterward, users can ask questions about their full meeting history, with answers linked to the moment when the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also catch users up on portions of a meeting they missed or were not paying attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow ’s custom dictionary, which helps with accuracy for acronyms, names, product names, and beyond, Wispr Notetaker “draws on the apps you connect, like Slack, and your calendar, to understand what this particular conversation is about,” says Kothari.

This also helps with automatic speaker attribution, which is particularly useful for meetings with several participants.

Wispr Notetaker transcribes meetings based on on-device audio capture, rather than joining calls as a separate participant.

It works across multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles, and has MCP support, allowing users to pull transcripts, summaries, and notes into Claude, ChatGPT, and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker is available beginning today on Mac, with a Windows version in development.

articles.title: 'The Guild' movie revival becomes highest-funded Kickstarter film ever, filling me with millennial nostalgia and making me very nervous
articles.subtitle: Massively multi-funded online roleplaying movie.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
As a millennial (boo, hiss) born in the 90s, I was just old enough to enjoy The Guild, a YouTube series about a group of dysfunctional MMO players, when it debuted online in 2007. 12-year-old me, who'd just gotten big into World of Warcraft and online games in general was downright invested—but that was then, and this is now.

I am currently 31 (also boo, also hiss) and I've got a lot less hair, which is part of why I was honestly surprised when I awoke to the news this week that The Guild: Ren Faire'd has become the highest-funded Kickstarter movie of all time—and one of the most successfully-funded movies to be fuelled by crowdfunding.

If you head on over to Kickstarter and apply the correct filters on its search function, you'll see it playing second fiddle to Critical Role: The Legend of Vox Machina 's animated "special"—which has since become a fully-fledged series spanning multiple seasons.

Originally asking for $1.5 million, the movie has brought in over $6.8 million at the time of writing. Now, this doesn't actually make it the highest-crowdfunded movie of all time by technicality —that award goes to 2025's David, which raised around $52 million, though that was achieved through asking for investors, rather than backers.

It was also based on a little book called The Bible, not a web series from 2007-2013 about World of Warcraft players. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit have a significant advantage when it comes to word of mouth.

"The Kickstarter is over. $6.8 million. You guys are incredible. Thank you for the support. The community. The creativity. We are so excited to make a movie and so much more for you guys," writes Felicia Day, who created the series itself. Day has since had a prolific career as an actress and the founder of Geek and Sundry, who we have to thank for the existence of Critical Role.

Which is cause for celebration! Though, I can't help but gnaw a little at my fingernails—The Guild was created originally in, quite literally, a different era, where MMOs were mysterious and inaccessible, and communities were more common. Heck, the OG series got picked up and streamed on Zune Marketplace and MSN Video. Remember those? I sure didn't.

And hey, maybe the Knights of Good going to the ren faire'll be a good laugh, but you'll either have to trade out most of the humour for jabs about how everything's on a Discord server now and high-end raids are datamined to death—or you'll have to become a little dated, only appealing to… well, people like me.

Which'll lead to three outcomes, two of which I dread: I'll be reminded of the sorry state of my favourite game genre by a bunch of actors who've aged better than me, I'll be mercilessly pandered to, or Felicia Day will successfully thread the needle and I'll have nothing to worry about. And hey, 45,500 people with $6.8 million bucks to spare aren't nearly as nervous. The Guild: Ren Faire'd plans to release sometime in 2027.

articles.subtitle: Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman reports that Apple is reorganizing parts of its brick-and-mortar stores this fall to make room for new home products.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman reports that Apple is reorganizing parts of its brick-and-mortar stores this fall to make room for new home products.

Writing in his latest Power On newsletter, Gurman says the teams responsible for store layouts are preparing changes to the "Avenues," or the perimeter walls in Apple's newer stores, where accessories like HomePod, Apple TV, AirPods, and Beats are displayed alongside third-party accessories.

The work is said to involve rearranging sections of the Avenues and adding accessory bays for upcoming new devices.

Apple is already believed to have an upgraded Apple TV and a new HomePod mini coming up. Gurman said in July that both were nearly ready, with faster chips for Siri AI but no major design changes. Rumors indicate an A17 Pro chip or better in the new Apple TV, and an S9-series chip, improved sound, and a red finish for the HomePod mini, the current version of which is now over 2,000 days old.

All of that being said, Gurman says the scale of the retail changes suggests prep-work for the launch of its long-awaited home hub with a display (aka the rumored HomePod with Display or "HomePad").

Gurman reported last month that the smart home hub will arrive at some point between October and early next year. It's expected to have a 7-inch square display, and will be sold with either a tabletop base or a wall mount. There's also said to be an all-new operating system built around tvOS with Siri AI powering the device.

Code strings uncovered in macOS Tahoe 26.7 last week suggest the home screen will use a Widget Gallery similar to the iPhone's Lock Screen customization options. The code also indicates that the new device's home screen could have many of the same options for icons, widgets, and clock faces, with widgets from a linked iPhone suggested automatically.

Apple will need a dedicated space where customers can see how the hub works, what its purpose is, and how it fits into the wider home setup, Gurman reports.

articles.title: OpenAI explains what will happen when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend
articles.subtitle: It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.

ChatGPT is the new ChatGPT Atlas

As we reported in July, OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser in favor of browser tools built into the new ChatGPT desktop app. Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 following a brief wind-down period.

OpenAI warns that Atlas may no longer open, browse, or support agentic workflows after that date. Because the discontinued browser will not continue receiving security updates, users will want to move to a supported alternative.

The transition may require some manual housekeeping for some. Atlas bookmarks will not transfer automatically. OpenAI recommends exporting bookmarks as an HTML file and saving important pages before Sunday’s deadline.

Cookies may have export options where available. ChatGPT conversation history is stored separately and will remain available.

AI browser alternatives

OpenAI is directing users toward the new ChatGPT desktop app. Its built-in browser supports multiple tabs, downloads, website logins, autofill, password management, extensions, and persistent browser state. However, it’s not exactly a browser-first experience.

The company recommends its Chrome extension when a task requires an existing Chrome profile, signed-in session, open tabs, or other extensions. ChatGPT’s desktop app also includes a “computer use” functionality that can optionally let it control Safari when granted permission.

There are plenty of other AI browser options on the Mac, including Comet, Dia, Opera Neon, and Aside. Anthropic is taking a similar two-track approach: Claude Code offers a sandboxed in-app browser, while its Chrome extension can work with existing logged-in sessions.
